title: Drupal site settings over JSON:API, per consumer
description: Four years ago I wrote that Drupal's JSON:API had no way to reach basic site configuration, and guessed the answer would involve the Consumers module and theme settings. Decoupled Settings 1.0.0-beta1 is that guess, built: allowlisted simple config over JSON:API, with every consumer able to override individual values.

content.html:
In April 2022 I wrote about decoupling configuration with Config Pages. It opened with a complaint that was true at the time:

While the Drupal JSON:API still doesn't provide any way to access basic site configuration, there are many ways it can be done...

And it closed with a promise:

One of my future experiments with Druxt will be to look at the options of using the Drupal Consumers module alongside Drupal theme settings as a solution.

That experiment is finished. It's called Decoupled Settings, and the first beta is on Drupal.org.

It reads the config Drupal already holds, exposes an allowlisted slice of it over JSON:API, and lets every Consumers entity override individual values. One backend, many frontends, each one rendering as its own site.

Core's JSON:API is a content API. It gets you entities: nodes, terms, users, media. It has never exposed simple configuration, and there's a reasonable argument that it shouldn't by default, because a lot of what lives in system.site and friends is not something you want readable by anyone who finds the endpoint.

But a decoupled frontend still needs the basics. The site name for the document title. The slogan. The logo and the favicon. The front page path, so the router knows what "home" resolves to. Right now every decoupled Drupal project solves that itself, and there are four common ways to do it, all of which I've used.

paragraphs.title: What we've all been doing instead

content.html: JSON:API Site exposes site information over JSON:API. It's the closest existing thing, and it's a hardcoded list of keys with no cacheability metadata on the response. If you want a key it doesn't know about, you patch it. If you want the response to invalidate when an editor changes the site name, you're on your own.

Config Pages is what my 2022 post was about, and it's still on my sites. You define a Config Page type, add whatever fields you want, and it comes out over JSON:API like any other entity. I wrote a Druxt module for consuming it.

I want to be clear that Decoupled Settings does not replace this. Config Pages is for settings you are inventing: the fields a single page app needs, a set of API keys, editorial toggles that have no home in Drupal's own config. That was the actual use case in the 2022 post, a calculator app fed configuration data from Drupal, and Config Pages is still the right answer for it.

What it's a clumsy fit for is settings Drupal already stores. Modelling the site name as a field on a Config Page means the site name now exists twice, and something has to keep the two in sync, and something eventually won't.
Site Settings has the same shape as Config Pages for these purposes: a content entity holding values you define. Same strength, same duplication.
JSON:API Extras reshapes resources that already exist. It can't conjure one for config that JSON:API never exposed.

Consumer Image Styles is the one that reframed the problem for me, because it had already answered the harder half of the question years ago: it varies its output per consumer. It just does it for image styles, not for settings.

The model is two sentences.

Global values are read from the config objects that already hold them. There is no second copy of the site name anywhere. An editor changes site information, and that is what a frontend reads on the next request. No sync step, nothing to drift.

A consumer stores only what it overrides. Tick a setting on a consumer, give it a value, and that consumer sees your value. Everything you didn't tick is inherited, and keeps following the site value when it changes. Overriding system.site:name for one frontend does not freeze that frontend's slogan.

What gets exposed at all is bounded twice. An administrator lists which config objects are exposed, and within those, typed config schema decides which keys appear and what primitive type they come out as. Keys with no schema are dropped rather than guessed at, which means a missing key is visible by its absence in the admin preview instead of failing silently at the frontend.

On install it exposes system.site and the active theme's settings, and nothing else.

paragraphs.title: "Not overridden" and "overridden to empty" are different things

content.html:
This is the small design decision the whole thing rests on, so it's worth calling out.

If a consumer has no slogan override, it inherits the site slogan. If a consumer has an override set to an empty string, it has deliberately no slogan, and that's what it gets. Clearing the override is a separate action that restores inheritance.

Internally that's the difference between array_key_exists() and isset(), and getting it wrong would make "this frontend shows no slogan" impossible to express. Every settings system I've built before this one got it wrong.

paragraphs.title: Decide who can read it before you turn it on

content.html:
This endpoint exposes site configuration, so the first thing to say about it is who can read it.

Reading requires the Read decoupled settings permission, and that permission is not granted to anonymous users on install. That's deliberate, and it means the module does nothing at all until you make a decision:

  • If the values are public (a site name and a logo that already appear on every rendered page), grant it to the anonymous role and let the frontend fetch without authenticating.
  • If they're not, grant it to a role reachable through an OAuth2 scope, and make the frontend authenticate as an app.

system.site:mail is on the exclusion list by default, because the site email address is the one key in system.site that nobody's frontend needs and spam bots very much want.
One JSON:API resource, built on JSON:API Resources. Ask it for the global values:
Or identify yourself as a consumer, by query parameter or by header:

A request that names no consumer, or names one that doesn't exist, reads the global values. The response says which consumer it resolved, so a frontend can tell the difference between "my overrides applied" and "my consumer ID was a typo":

The logo and favicon are resolved URLs, through core's own theme settings resolution, with core's fallbacks. Not raw config paths that the frontend then has to know how to turn into something fetchable.

Responses carry the config cache tags of every object that contributed, plus a cache context per negotiation mechanism. Change the site name and the caches that hold a response built from it are invalidated, without anyone writing a hook.

paragraphs.title: The OAuth client is the consumer

content.html:
This is my favourite detail, and I can't take credit for it, because it falls out of how Simple OAuth and Consumers already fit together.

Ask for a token with client_credentials and then use it:

content.title: As an authenticated app
content.code:
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST https://backend.example.com/oauth/token \
  -d grant_type=client_credentials \
  -d client_id=partner_frontend \
  -d client_secret=SECRET \
  -d scope=frontend_app | jq -r .access_token)

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://backend.example.com/jsonapi/decoupled/settings

content.html: No consumerId, no X-Consumer-ID. Simple OAuth sets the consumer identity on the request from the token's own consumer, so the app is identified by the token alone. The OAuth client and the settings consumer are one entity doing both jobs.

Worth knowing before you wire this up: Simple OAuth 6 resolves no default scope for client_credentials, so machine auth needs three things set up once. An oauth2_scope entity with the client_credentials grant enabled and role granularity pointing at a role that holds the read permission. A confidential consumer with a secret, client_credentials in its grant types, that scope named in client_credentials_scopes, and a user_id for the account the token acts as. And scope= on the token request itself.

Miss the last one and you get a token that authenticates fine and is allowed to do nothing.

A companion Druxt module is in review, so I'll describe what it does rather than tell you to install it yet.

At build time it identifies the app as a consumer, optionally gets a client_credentials token, reads the settings endpoint as that consumer, and bakes the result into the build's runtime config. The consumer's site name becomes the document title template, and the theme's resolved favicon replaces the static one.

That's the app authenticating, not a user. druxt-auth covers the user login flow, and nothing covered the build-time flow before this.

The logo and favicon get served from the frontend's own origin, by a server middleware whose allowlist is exactly the files the settings name. Nothing outside that list is reachable through it. It's a proxy to named files, not a proxy to the backend, and it means the Drupal install needs no public exposure for its assets.

paragraphs.title: Two frontends, one backend, same code

content.html: The demo is two builds of an identical codebase:

content.title: Two builds, one repository
content.code:
DRUXT_CONSUMER_ID=public_frontend  NUXT_BUILD_DIR=.nuxt-public  PORT=3005 npm run build && npm start

DRUXT_CONSUMER_ID=partner_frontend NUXT_BUILD_DIR=.nuxt-partner PORT=3007 npm run build && npm start

content.html:
One comes up as "Druxt Public" with the Olivero logo. The other comes up as "Partner Portal" with the Drupal logo. Nothing in the repository differs between them.

The separate build directories matter, and they're not a workaround. The head is baked into the build, which is the model working as designed: settings are frozen into the artifact like any other static build input, and changing a setting means a rebuild. Exactly as it would if you'd used environment variables, except that a content editor can do it from Drupal.

Back in 2022 I described wanting "one Drupal backend for many targeted consumers" and said I found the other side of that coin more interesting, one frontend for many backends. Four years on I'll take the first one. It's the version people keep actually asking me for.

This is 1.0.0-beta1, and the beta is deliberate rather than a formality. Three things gate a stable release:

  1. Per-consumer include and exclude lists, either built or explicitly deferred with the storage shape confirmed as additive.
  2. A second real consumer of the API, beyond the Druxt module. One integration is not enough to know whether the shape is right.
  3. A beta soak on real sites.

Two limitations worth knowing about up front, because neither is a bug I'm going to quietly fix:

Anonymous basics plus authenticated extras at once isn't expressible. You can serve a public set of settings, or a protected set, but not "everyone gets the site name, authenticated apps also get these three" from one site. Per-consumer include and exclude is the designed answer and it isn't built.

Translation and language negotiation of exposed values aren't handled. If your settings are translated, this doesn't know about it yet.

On testing: the module runs 89 tests and 435 assertions across unit, kernel and functional coverage, and the full suite passes on both Drupal 10 and Drupal 11. The security behaviour is covered over real HTTP with both page caches enabled, including the case that matters most, that two consumers identified by header never share a cached response.

The first DrupalCI pipeline on Drupal.org came back green across all eight jobs, which I'm choosing to enjoy rather than examine too closely.

content.description: Issue queue on Drupal.org, mirror on GitHub. If you're running decoupled Drupal and you've solved site settings some other way, I'd like to hear how before the API shape sets in a stable release.
